headline: IPO failed due to gap between operational achievements and valuation asked, with unproven data centre expansions in new jurisdictions announced only months before listing
reasoning: Frazis believes the Firmus $40B IPO collapsed because investors identified a material gap between what the company had actually achieved operationally and the valuation being demanded. The company was ascribing significant value to data centre operations that had only been announced in the last few months, in jurisdictions where they had no prior operational track record. Information about these concerns leaked slowly through the press over the course of the week, leading fund managers to withdraw one by one. Frazis notes that a more open, transparent approach to disclosure would have served the company better and will likely be required in any future IPO attempt. He believes the personal background of co-founder Oliver Curtis was largely irrelevant to investor decisions; the numbers and documents were what mattered.
quote: They were ascribing a lot of value to operations that were only announced month in the last few months in jurisdictions which they hadn't operated in. You know, I feel like these were the material facts that really swung things rather than, you know, the personal history of anyone. I really think a more open approach would have served them better, and it's probably something they'll need to do next time if they want to be successful.
episode_title: Frazis on the red flags that killed Firmus' $40B IPO

headline: IPO pulled due to overvalued pricing, misleading EBIT metrics, insider derivative sell provisions, and failure of offshore demand to convert to real commitments
reasoning: Frazis argues the Firmus IPO failed for multiple reasons: the price was too high relative to cash being raised, and the EBIT figure promoted to investors excluded corporate costs, was two years forward, required unsecured additional funding, and was not calculated in a standard way. Derivative agreements allowed founders and insiders to sell despite public messaging that they were locked up. Offshore indications of interest did not convert to hard cash commitments. He notes that even if you made the $40B valuation work, investors in a high-risk deal need to see 2-3x upside, which was too much of a stretch. The late-stage attempt to lower the price was too little too late as the deal had lost momentum.
quote: I think there are a lot of details that were in the prospectus that weren't shared or weren't, weren't easily available. You know, there are many journalists saying they weren't able to access the documents the entire period. There was a lot of information in the fine print that was kind of different to what was being shared publicly and what, what the kind of message from the bankers running the deal was that change change the facts materially. For example, the EBIT number that was thrown around had a lot of caveats. It excluded corporate costs. It's not really how you normally calculate EBIT. It was two years in advance, required additional funding that wasn't yet secured. There were derivative agreements allowed, which allowed founders and insiders to sell, whereas the reporting otherwise was saying, you know, they're, they're only out to sell 10% a year later. But this enabled them to to sell in with, with derivatives effectively.

headline: Better risk-reward than most near-cloud AI infrastructure plays; real customers are hyperscalers and governments, not near-clouds
reasoning: Frazis argues that NVIDIA's actual business is driven by hyperscalers and governments, not near-cloud customers. While near-clouds carry high risk of technological obsolescence and leverage, NVIDIA itself sits upstream of that risk. Even amid uncertainty over GPU longevity and market share, NVIDIA offers a better risk-reward than most AI infrastructure lenders or near-cloud operators.
quote: Even NVIDIA itself, you know, ultimately Nvidia's real business is not near clouds. They're trying to foster these new customers as much as they can, but the real customers are the hyper scalers and governments, and so even even NVIDIA would, I think, be a better risk reward than most of the near clouds.

headline: Rational backer of Firmus but ultimately a supplier receiving cash, not a true partner; strategy to cultivate customers beyond hyperscalers who are building their own chips
reasoning: Frazis notes that NVIDIA invested equity in Firmus and helped secure debt financing via contract terms, but at its core NVIDIA is a supplier being paid by Firmus to purchase and install its chips. NVIDIA publicly backed Firmus and Jensen Huang name-dropped the company on stage as part of an explicit strategy to foster customers beyond the hyperscalers, who are increasingly developing their own chips. Frazis says this makes him want to be NVIDIA, implying NVIDIA benefits most from the arrangement regardless of Firmus's outcome.
quote: Well, ultimately NVIDIA is a receiver of cash from Firmus, you know, so they were, they were contributing, they've invested equity, they were helping them get the debt with their contract terms with offers to buy back capacity. So they're a partner. But really they're they're a customer of NVIDIA. And it makes me want to be NVIDIA. There's been explicit strategy of NVIDIA. They've publicly gone on record supporting firmus. Jensen Huang called them out by name on stage in the United States, you know, recently Nvidia's trying to foster additional customers on top of the hyper scalers which are developing their own chips and looking to move more and more of their demand onto their own technology stack.

headline: GPU technological obsolescence is a real medium-term risk: NVIDIA on annual cadence, hyperscalers and OpenAI building own chips, and inference-optimised startups threatening general-purpose GPU economics over 3-5 years
reasoning: Frazis highlights that NVIDIA has moved to an annual chip generation cadence, meaning GPUs bought today will face multiple newer, more capable successors within the typical asset financing horizon. Beyond NVIDIA, hyperscalers are all developing proprietary silicon, OpenAI has its own chip program, and well-funded VC startups are designing inference-specific chips that could be faster, cheaper and more energy-efficient than NVIDIA's general-purpose GPUs. This makes current-generation GPUs poor collateral for long-dated lending or investment.
quote: NVIDIA themselves have moved to an annual cadence, so they're bringing out entirely new generation every year now. So over four or five years, you know, of the of the mid to long term, there'll be a number of new more efficient, more capable reviews supplied by NVIDIA themselves. And it's an open question as to how fast that innovation will go. And it's not just NVIDIA, you know, the hyperscale is all developing their own chips, Open AI is developing their own chip and there are a number of very well funded VC start UPS developing new designs. Nvidia's chips are mostly general purpose. You can train and do inference, but from first principles, you should be able to design A chip that can just do inference more efficiently, faster, better, more cost efficiently as well lower energy requirements if you just design it for that one thing. And that's broadly where the market is going.

headline: Avoided at $40B+ valuation on $50M revenue — GPU collateral obsolescence risk, extreme leverage, opaque prospectus, and misaligned public messaging made it uninvestable at the offer price
reasoning: Frazis outlines multiple red flags that killed Firmus's IPO: the business is highly capital-intensive and heavily leveraged, with most assets invested in GPUs that depreciate rapidly and face technological obsolescence as NVIDIA moves to annual chip generations and hyperscalers develop proprietary chips. The company generated only ~$50M in revenue yet sought a $40B+ valuation. He also criticises the lack of transparency — key details buried in the prospectus materially changed the public narrative, documents were not made widely available, and fund managers gradually withdrew as more information leaked. He believes a lower valuation and more open price discovery process could have saved the deal.
quote: I think they need to temper the valuation expectations #1 I'm sure they will #2 you know, obviously it's going to delay the process. It means there's a lot of numbers in our public, if they come back in three, 612 months, whatever it is, on the NASDAQ or the SX or elsewhere or privately. And they've made material progress, they're making money. They've grown revenue. Revenues are somewhat proportionate to the value. I mean, there's a company that just did 50 mil of revenue last year, right, coming out at over $40 billion. They're asking for. That's a huge ask. It's a huge leap of faith. You know, they need to bring those numbers closer, probably on both sides, probably execute better and also bring the valuation expectations down. That would definitely make it a lot more attractive. And I still think at a lower valuation, this probably could have got away.

headline: Sidestep GPU obsolescence risk by going upstream — memory, testing, power, and chip manufacturing win regardless of which AI architecture prevails
reasoning: Frazis notes that regardless of whether NVIDIA, hyperscalers or AI startups win the chip design race, the underlying manufacturing, testing, memory and power supply chain must still be used. He sees these upstream semiconductor companies as a way to gain AI exposure without having to answer the difficult question of which GPU generation will retain value or which company will dominate inference chips. Companies in the semiconductor space that serve all these customers should win regardless of the outcome.
quote: Well, you can kind of go upstream of that, right? So whether it's NVIDIA or Hyperscaler or a startup, those chips are still going to need to be made somewhere. It's still going to need to be tested. There's very few companies that can do that. They'll still need memory, they'll still need power. There's a number of ways you can invest in AI and sidestep the question over what will Nvidia's market share be or is the current generation of GPU's going to be worth much in five years time? You know, they're difficult, very difficult questions to answer and you have to risk and price them appropriately because of those those question marks. But there are companies, many companies in the semiconductor space that should win regardless.
